chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
title: Buying DownBeat polls
summary: Hampton had truckloads of tearsheets bought to win the poll; Mingus put in Red Callender's name.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: I got DownBeat in there some kind of way. In those days, That's something else about cheating, man; those polls they used to have, Lionel always, (inaudible). ^ A truck backed up to a theater stage where we were playing. We had a week in the theater, and a truck backed up and dumped off some DownBeat magazines. Except n't said they were magazines. They were tearsheets from the poll. Also, I blew for a half-hour. He got everybody voted for Hamp. to do it. But that year Red Callender got a whole lot of votes because I couldn't bring myself to put my own name down on Callender's bass, so I put Red Calloway's name down. He almost upset the polls.
But Benny Goodman was there then, too, so he bought more DownBeats than anybody, so he won.
They used to buy whole truckloads of DownBeats?
Yeah. You didn't know about that?
No. I've heard about people buying --
Yeah, They bought the votes. They bought a truckload.
That's great. A little history is made here today, folks. How to win the DownBeat poll.

Makes a lot of sense. Well, they've been doing that one way or another every time there's a poll. In The movies, the -- everybody who works for Columbia better vote for "Close Encounters" or they're out of a job. Silly.
In those days, DownBeat carried a little weight.
Don't hardly carry much weight now.
